title: How To Think About AI: A Guide for the Perplexed
author: Richard Susskind

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source partly aligns with the cluster on unreliability, over-reliance and measured governance, but shifts the central frame from present task-level capability and selective human-led deployment to uncertain technological trajectories, legal exceptionalism and potentially deeper transformation through innovation, problem elimination and replacement of litigation.
qs: Susskind makes a convincing case — to me, at any rate — that using AI to implement different approaches to conflict resolution or prevention of legal problems could reduce or replace litigation as we know it.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts that AI changes legal work through task substitution and process redesign, then materially extends the cluster by distinguishing automation from innovation and elimination. It predicts that AI-enabled prevention and alternative dispute resolution could ultimately reduce or replace conventional litigation, while presenting this as a forward-looking claim rather than evidence of current profession-wide displacement.
qs: This includes distinguishing three concepts:  - Automation (task substitution) is about finding a way to be more efficient about doing what we are doing now.

Susskind makes a convincing case — to me, at any rate — that using AI to implement different approaches to conflict resolution or prevention of legal problems could reduce or replace litigation as we know it.

kp.k: Mental models rather than definitive answers
kp.d: The reviewer presents Susskind’s 2025 book as a conceptual guide for lawyers and policymakers, not a set of solutions or an ethics compliance manual. Its contribution is to clarify questions about AI without either wholesale enthusiasm or rejection.
qs: This is not a book of answers. It is a book of questions.
His goal is to help readers identify the issues and suggest some clear ways of thinking about them.

kp.k: Current capabilities are not the limit of future AI
kp.d: Susskind predicts that current technologies will appear primitive within years and argues that forecasts neglect technologies not yet invented. The review relates this outlook to recurring cycles of overpromising, backlash and progress, and reports accelerating technological returns as a possible mechanism rather than presenting a measured legal-sector forecast.
qs: In not many years, our current technologies will look primitive, much as our 1980s kit appears antiquated today.
Most predictions about the future are in my view irredeemably flawed because they ignore the not yet invented technologies.
Information technologies like computing get exponentially cheaper because each advance makes it easier to design the next stage of their own evolution.

kp.k: Useful outcomes need not replicate human reasoning
kp.d: The review reports Susskind’s distinction between process-thinking and outcome-thinking, using his interpretation of Chomsky’s and Kissinger’s contrasting views. The reviewer applies this framework to lawyers: attention to how AI works may obscure practical benefits when machines produce desired results through unfamiliar methods.
qs: Susskind’s explanation for the contrasts is that Kissinger focuses on outputs, while Chomsky focuses on process:
machines don’t need to copy us to deliver the outcomes or outputs that customers, clients and users want from their providers.
Lawyers, trained to analyze process, may be predisposed to dismiss AI’s unfamiliar logic, missing the forest (useful results) for the trees (alien methods).

kp.k: Professional exceptionalism can obscure displacement risks
kp.d: Susskind’s reported “Not-Us” critique identifies a cross-professional tendency to recognise AI’s potential elsewhere while resisting its applicability at home. Lawyers’ claims of limited suitability for legal practice are presented as an instance of this conceptual bias, not as findings from a specified empirical study.
qs: Professionals see much greater scope for AI in disciplines other than their own.

Lawyers assert confidently that audit, journalism and management consulting are ripe for displacement but offer special pleadings on its very limited suitability in the practice of law and the administration of justice.

kp.k: Human traits may have functional machine substitutes
kp.d: The review reports Susskind’s argument that AI can provide quasi-judgment, quasi-empathy and quasi-creativity without possessing their human forms. The reviewer finds his case for some superior machine capabilities convincing and uses it to challenge professional confidence in irreplaceability; the document supplies no comparative measurements.
qs: For example, AI skeptics are fond of saying that computers can never replace them because they don’t have the same judgment, empathy and creativity.
Susskind demonstrates — quite convincingly — that the computer versions of these biological traits can be superior in several ways to the human version.

kp.k: Innovation and prevention could disrupt litigation beyond automation
kp.d: The review distinguishes task substitution from delivering outcomes through radically different processes and from eliminating the underlying problem. It presents innovation and elimination as potentially greater employment threats than automation. The reviewer endorses Susskind’s prospective argument that AI-enabled conflict resolution or prevention could reduce or replace existing litigation, without claiming demonstrated displacement.
qs: Automation (task substitution) is about finding a way to be more efficient about doing what we are doing now.
Innovation means delivering the outcomes clients want, using techniques or technology that support radically new underlying processes.
Elimination means not just solving a problem but eliminating it.

Susskind makes a convincing case — to me, at any rate — that using AI to implement different approaches to conflict resolution or prevention of legal problems could reduce or replace litigation as we know it.

kp.k: Risk analysis includes unreliability, dependence and inaction
kp.d: The review reproduces Susskind’s seven-category framework: existential, catastrophe, political, socio-economic, unreliability, reliance and inaction risks. It distinguishes errors from inappropriate trust and includes the costs of withholding beneficial AI alongside employment, inequality and governance concerns. This is a conceptual classification, not a measurement of risk incidence.
qs: Category 4: Socio-Economic Risks Effects on employment, inequality, social cohesion, and bias.
Category 5: Risks of Unreliability Issues arising from AI errors, inaccuracies, or “hallucinations.”
Category 6: Risks of Reliance Dangers of over-dependence or inappropriate trust in AI systems.
Category 7: Risks of Inaction Negative consequences of failing to develop or deploy beneficial AI.

kp.k: Governance requires urgency without assuming inevitable catastrophe
kp.d: The review characterises Susskind’s recommendation as measured urgency. His explicitly speculative conclusion suggests at least a decade to decide and act on humanity’s desired future, potentially through law, while emphasising the importance of reactions over the next few years. This is a normative and prospective argument rather than an established intervention deadline.
qs: He emphasizes measured urgency rather than end-of-the-world hysteria.

My guess is that we have at least a decade to decide what we want for humanity and then to act upon that decision — if necessary, emphatically and pre-emptively — through nation and international law.
[O]ur future will depend largely on how we react over the next few years.

kp.k: The reviewer connects conceptual understanding to professional duties
kp.d: The reviewer describes ABA Formal Opinion 512 as applying obligations concerning competence, confidentiality, communication, candor, supervision and reasonable fees to AI use. The article connects Susskind’s capabilities discussion to Model Rule 1.1, his risk framework to Rule 1.6, and process-versus-outcome thinking to Rules 1.4 and 3.3. These are the reviewer’s applications of the book, which is expressly not an ethics compliance manual.
qs: While not an ethics compliance manual, Susskind’s book offers precisely the conceptual tools — the “mental models” — needed to navigate these practical obligations.

His structured analysis of AI risks (Chapters 8 and 9) provides a framework for assessing potential threats to *confidentiality* under Rule 1.6, particularly concerning data security and inadvertent disclosure when using third-party AI tools.

Exploring the “process vs. outcome” distinction (Chapter 3) can illuminate challenges in *communicating* AI use to clients (Rule 1.4) or ensuring *candor* to tribunals (Rule 3.3) about the origins and reliability of AI-generated materials.

kp.k: Tool proliferation strengthens the case for conceptual literacy
kp.d: The review reports that LegalTech Hub cataloged over 500 generative AI apps for lawyers in March 2025. It uses this count to argue that nuanced understanding matters more than obtaining another application; the count describes tool availability, not adoption or demonstrated effects on legal employment.
qs: With over [500 generative AI apps for lawyers](https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/contents/lth-genai-legal-tech-map-march-2025/) cataloged by [LegalTech Hub](https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/) in March 2025, the proliferation of such tools shows no signs of slowing.
In this environment, nuanced understanding is more critical than simply another application.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The reviewer argues that AI's effects extend beyond automating existing legal tasks: new methods of resolving or preventing disputes could reduce or replace conventional litigation.
pts.d: The unnamed reviewer endorses the argument presented in Susskind's book that innovation and elimination of underlying problems may threaten jobs more than task substitution. This is a conditional prediction about changing legal services, not a reported instance of litigation already being displaced. The reviewer also argues that lawyers' focus on human processes can obscure AI's useful outputs and that computer analogues of judgment, empathy and creativity challenge assumptions of professional irreplaceability.

pts.k: The reviewer presents AI use as requiring lawyers to operationalize professional duties concerning competence, confidentiality, communication, candor, supervision and fees.
pts.d: The reviewer invokes ABA Formal Opinion 512 and argues that the book's conceptual models help lawyers apply these duties to AI. These are the reviewer's practical connections between the book and legal ethics, rather than claims that the book itself is an ethics compliance manual. The reviewer also describes legal AI tools as proliferating.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is principally the reviewer's endorsement of Susskind's conceptual arguments, supplemented by an ethics authority and a dated tool inventory.
pts.d: The review does not provide empirical measurements of litigation displacement, employment effects or AI superiority in judgment, empathy or creativity. It points readers to the book's arguments, especially Chapter 5 and Chapters 6–7. ABA Formal Opinion 512 supplies the cited authority for the discussion of professional obligations. LegalTech Hub's March 2025 inventory of more than 500 generative AI applications for lawyers supports the claim of tool proliferation, not the predicted displacement of legal work. No benchmarks or case studies establishing that displacement are reported.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Legal-service displacement has no specified deadline and depends on AI enabling new approaches; ethical adaptation is presented as a current need.
pts.d: The litigation prediction is expressly qualified by 'could' and by the condition that AI be used for different approaches to conflict resolution or prevention. The tool inventory is dated March 2025. The reviewer describes rapid technological development and near-term policy choices with long-term consequences, but supplies no quantified forecast for legal employment, adoption or litigation volumes. The decade-long decision window quoted from the book concerns humanity's wider response to AI, not a timetable for replacing lawyers.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The review identifies lawyers, litigation practitioners, clients, policymakers and the public as affected, without distinguishing firm sizes or legal-market tiers.
pts.d: Lawyers face potential changes to their tasks and professional roles, and a need to understand AI rather than assume their capabilities are irreplaceable. Litigation practitioners could face reduced demand for conventional dispute resolution if prevention or alternative processes succeed. Clients are implicated through desired outcomes, confidentiality and communication; tribunals through the reliability of AI-generated materials. Policymakers and the public face choices about deployment and risk. The source does not specify effects on associate-to-partner ratios, particular firm types, ALSPs or in-house legal departments.
